claim: Adherens junction (AJ) assembly under force is essential for epithelial monolayer bending, collective cell migration, cell extrusion and wound healing.
source: Adherens junction (AJ) assembly under force is essential for many biological processes like epithelial monolayer bending, collective cell migration, cell extrusion and wound healing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these biological processes.

claim: The acto-myosin cytoskeleton acts as a major force-generator during the de novo formation and remodeling of AJ.
source: The acto-myosin cytoskeleton acts as a major force-generator during the de novo formation and remodeling of AJ.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about acto-myosin function.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB differentially regulate biogenesis of AJ through association with distinct actin networks.
source: NMIIA and NMIIB differentially regulate biogenesis of AJ through association with distinct actin networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including immunostaining, SIM microscopy, and functional assays.

claim: NMIIA provides the mechanical tugging force necessary for cell-cell junction reinforcement and maintenance.
source: Analysis of junction dynamics, actin organization, and mechanical forces of control and knockdown cells for myosins revealed that NMIIA provides the mechanical tugging force necessary for cell-cell junction reinforcement and maintenance.
evidence: This claim is supported by traction force microscopy data and junction stability assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: NMIIB is involved in E-cadherin clustering.
source: NMIIB is involved in E-cadherin clustering, maintenance of a branched actin layer connecting E-cadherin complexes and perijunctional actin fibres leading to the building-up of anisotropic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data, SIM microscopy, and E-cadherin substrate experiments.

claim: NMIIB maintains a branched actin layer connecting E-cadherin complexes and perijunctional actin fibres.
source: NMIIB is involved in E-cadherin clustering, maintenance of a branched actin layer connecting E-cadherin complexes and perijunctional actin fibres leading to the building-up of anisotropic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy showing NMIIB localization with branched actin and cortactin.

claim: NMIIB leads to the building-up of anisotropic stress at adherens junctions.
source: NMIIB is involved in E-cadherin clustering, maintenance of a branched actin layer connecting E-cadherin complexes and perijunctional actin fibres leading to the building-up of anisotropic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis from traction force microscopy data.

claim: AJ mediated by E-cadherin/catenin complexes are key elements of epithelial cell-cell adhesions.
source: AJ mediated by E-cadherin/catenin complexes are key elements of epithelial cell-cell adhesions and the first ones to assemble upon contact initiation (Adams et al., 1998; Green et al., 2010; Takeichi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: E-cadherin/catenin complexes are the first adhesions to assemble upon contact initiation.
source: AJ mediated by E-cadherin/catenin complexes are key elements of epithelial cell-cell adhesions and the first ones to assemble upon contact initiation (Adams et al., 1998; Green et al., 2010; Takeichi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adherens junctions provide strong mechanical coupling between neighboring cells through association with the acto-myosin cytoskeleton.
source: They provide strong mechanical coupling between neighboring cells through association with the acto-myosin cytoskeleton (Mège and Ishiyama, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for cell-cell rearrangement.
source: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for cell-cell rearrangement (Cavey et al., 2008; Maître et al., 2015), tissue closure (Jacinto et al., 2002) and the maintenance of epithelial cell integrity during wound healing or cell extrusion (Harris et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for tissue closure.
source: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for cell-cell rearrangement (Cavey et al., 2008; Maître et al., 2015), tissue closure (Jacinto et al., 2002) and the maintenance of epithelial cell integrity during wound healing or cell extrusion (Harris et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for the maintenance of epithelial cell integrity during wound healing or cell extrusion.
source: The assembly of de novo AJ is crucial for cell-cell rearrangement (Cavey et al., 2008; Maître et al., 2015), tissue closure (Jacinto et al., 2002) and the maintenance of epithelial cell integrity during wound healing or cell extrusion (Harris et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Initial contact between facing lamellipodia induces immediate clustering of cadherin molecules by trans- and cis-oligomerization during de novo cell-cell contact formation.
source: During de novo cell-cell contact formation, initial contact between facing lamellipodia induces immediate clustering of cadherin molecules by trans- and cis-oligomerization (Adams et al., 1998; Yap et al., 1997; Strale et al., 2015; Mège et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Signaling events involving Rho GTPases trigger local remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton through Arp2/3- or formin-mediated actin polarization in the vicinity of AJs.
source: Subsequent signaling events involving Rho GTPases trigger local remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton through Arp2/3- or formin-mediated actin polarization in the vicinity of AJs (Grikscheit et al., 2015; Kovacs et al., 2002; Yamada and Nelson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cytoskeletal rearrangements drive the expansion of cell-cell contacts and inter-cellular adhesion strengthening.
source: These cytoskeletal rearrangements drive the expansion of cell-cell contacts and inter-cellular adhesion strengthening (Green et al., 2010; Krendel and Bonder, 1999; Chu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Non-muscle Myosin II (NMII) is a fundamental player in force-generation and force-transmission at AJ both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Non-muscle Myosin II (NMII) has emerged as a fundamental player in force-generation and force-transmission at AJ both in vitro and in vivo (Borghi et al., 2012; Curran et al., 2017; Ladoux and Mège, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue architecture.
source: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue architecture (Salomon et al., 2017), epithelial tissue morphogenesis (Munjal and Lecuit, 2014), tissue repair (Tamada et al., 2007; Begnaud et al., 2016) and cell extrusion (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue morphogenesis.
source: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue architecture (Salomon et al., 2017), epithelial tissue morphogenesis (Munjal and Lecuit, 2014), tissue repair (Tamada et al., 2007; Begnaud et al., 2016) and cell extrusion (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII is essential for tissue repair.
source: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue architecture (Salomon et al., 2017), epithelial tissue morphogenesis (Munjal and Lecuit, 2014), tissue repair (Tamada et al., 2007; Begnaud et al., 2016) and cell extrusion (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII is essential for cell extrusion.
source: NMII is essential for epithelial tissue architecture (Salomon et al., 2017), epithelial tissue morphogenesis (Munjal and Lecuit, 2014), tissue repair (Tamada et al., 2007; Begnaud et al., 2016) and cell extrusion (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII protects junctions from disassembly during development.
source: NMII protects junctions from disassembly during development (Weng and Wieschaus, 2016) and provides the mechanical tugging force necessary for AJ reinforcement (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII provides the mechanical tugging force necessary for AJ reinforcement.
source: NMII protects junctions from disassembly during development (Weng and Wieschaus, 2016) and provides the mechanical tugging force necessary for AJ reinforcement (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In endothelial cells, NMII is recruited early in filopodia-mediated bridge bundles.
source: In endothelial cells, NMII is recruited early in filopodia-mediated bridge bundles and its activity is required for accumulation of VE-cadherin in nascent AJs (Hoelzle and Svitkina, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMII activity is required for accumulation of VE-cadherin in nascent AJs in endothelial cells.
source: In endothelial cells, NMII is recruited early in filopodia-mediated bridge bundles and its activity is required for accumulation of VE-cadherin in nascent AJs (Hoelzle and Svitkina, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In epithelial cells, NMII favors local concentration of E-cadherin at cell-cell contacts.
source: In epithelial cells, NMII favors local concentration of E-cadherin at cell-cell contacts (Shewan et al., 2005; Smutny et al., 2010) and it is enriched at the edges of elongating junctions where it drives contact expansion in response to RhoA (Yamada and Nelson, 2007; Krendel and Bonder, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMII is enriched at the edges of elongating junctions where it drives contact expansion in response to RhoA.
source: In epithelial cells, NMII favors local concentration of E-cadherin at cell-cell contacts (Shewan et al., 2005; Smutny et al., 2010) and it is enriched at the edges of elongating junctions where it drives contact expansion in response to RhoA (Yamada and Nelson, 2007; Krendel and Bonder, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, NMII heavy chains exist as three different isoforms: NMIIA, NMIIB and NMIIC encoded by MYH9, MYH10 and MYH14 genes, respectively.
source: In mammalian cells, NMII heavy chains exist as three different isoforms: NMIIA, NMIIB and NMIIC encoded by MYH9, MYH10 and MYH14 genes, respectively (Conti and Adelstein, 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB are widely expressed whereas NMIIC is not detected in several tissues.
source: NMIIA and NMIIB are widely expressed whereas NMIIC is not detected in several tissues (Ma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB isoforms have been assigned both redundant and specific functions depending on cell types and processes.
source: Despite structural similarities, NMIIA and NMIIB isoforms have been assigned both redundant and specific functions depending on cell types and processes (Beach and Hammer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB exhibit different ATPase activities and actin-binding properties.
source: NMIIA and NMIIB exhibit different ATPase activities and actin-binding properties (Wang et al., 2003; Kovács et al., 2003; Kovács et al., 2007; Billington et al., 2013), in addition to their specific C-terminal tails that confer them unique functions (Sandquist and Means, 2008; Juanes-Garcia et al., 2015; Chang and Kumar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB have specific C-terminal tails that confer them unique functions.
source: NMIIA and NMIIB exhibit different ATPase activities and actin-binding properties (Wang et al., 2003; Kovács et al., 2003; Kovács et al., 2007; Billington et al., 2013), in addition to their specific C-terminal tails that confer them unique functions (Sandquist and Means, 2008; Juanes-Garcia et al., 2015; Chang and Kumar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB can exist as activated monomers in cells.
source: These two isoforms can exist as activated monomers in cells, but they can also co-assemble as homotypic and heterotypic filaments (Shutova et al., 2014; Beach et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB can co-assemble as homotypic and heterotypic filaments.
source: These two isoforms can exist as activated monomers in cells, but they can also co-assemble as homotypic and heterotypic filaments (Shutova et al., 2014; Beach et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB play both unique and overlapping roles in vivo.
source: NMIIA and NMIIB play both unique and overlapping roles in vivo (Skoglund et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; Haque et al., 2017; Ridge et al., 2017; Conti et al., 2004; Tullio et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In cells migrating on 2D surfaces, NMIIA localizes at the cell front.
source: In cells migrating on 2D surfaces, NMIIA localizes at the cell front, limits lamellipodial protrusive activity and reduces 2D cell migration speed by regulating focal adhesions dynamics and traction forces (Doyle et al., 2012; Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA limits lamellipodial protrusive activity in cells migrating on 2D surfaces.
source: In cells migrating on 2D surfaces, NMIIA localizes at the cell front, limits lamellipodial protrusive activity and reduces 2D cell migration speed by regulating focal adhesions dynamics and traction forces (Doyle et al., 2012; Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA reduces 2D cell migration speed by regulating focal adhesions dynamics and traction forces.
source: In cells migrating on 2D surfaces, NMIIA localizes at the cell front, limits lamellipodial protrusive activity and reduces 2D cell migration speed by regulating focal adhesions dynamics and traction forces (Doyle et al., 2012; Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB localizes at the cell rear in cells migrating on 2D surfaces.
source: NMIIB localizes at the cell rear and is required for front-back polarity and tail retraction (Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Kolega, 2003; Sandquist et al., 2006; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Betapudi, 2010; Shutova et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB is required for front-back polarity and tail retraction in cells migrating on 2D surfaces.
source: NMIIB localizes at the cell rear and is required for front-back polarity and tail retraction (Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Kolega, 2003; Sandquist et al., 2006; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Betapudi, 2010; Shutova et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In 3D, NMIIA favors cell displacement.
source: In 3D, NMIIA favors cell displacement (Doyle et al., 2012; Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Shih and Yamada, 2010) while NMIIB drives nuclear translocation (Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In 3D, NMIIB drives nuclear translocation.
source: In 3D, NMIIA favors cell displacement (Doyle et al., 2012; Betapudi et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2006; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Shih and Yamada, 2010) while NMIIB drives nuclear translocation (Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB plays a determinant role in durotaxis.
source: NMIIB also plays a determinant role in durotaxis (Raab et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB both localize at apical junction complexes of polarized MCF-7 cells.
source: Yap and collaborators have reported that NMIIA and NMIIB both localize at apical junction complexes of polarized MCF-7 cells (Smutny et al., 2010; Gomez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA may favor the accumulation of E-cadherin in the AJ belt in MCF-7 cells.
source: Upon specific isoform expression silencing, they further proposed that NMIIA may favor the accumulation of E-cadherin in the AJ belt while NMIIB may stabilize the associated perijunctional actin ring, reinforce junctions and prevent them from disruptive forces (Smutny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB may stabilize the associated perijunctional actin ring in MCF-7 cells.
source: Upon specific isoform expression silencing, they further proposed that NMIIA may favor the accumulation of E-cadherin in the AJ belt while NMIIB may stabilize the associated perijunctional actin ring, reinforce junctions and prevent them from disruptive forces (Smutny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB may reinforce junctions and prevent them from disruptive forces in MCF-7 cells.
source: Upon specific isoform expression silencing, they further proposed that NMIIA may favor the accumulation of E-cadherin in the AJ belt while NMIIB may stabilize the associated perijunctional actin ring, reinforce junctions and prevent them from disruptive forces (Smutny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA was required to assemble junctional complexes using CRISPR-Cas9 gene invalidation.
source: Ozawa reported using CRISPR-Cas9 gene invalidation that NMIIA was required to assemble junctional complexes (Ozawa, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA associates with contractile actin bundle running parallel to linear AJ in endothelial cells.
source: Svitkina and collaborators reported an association of NMIIA with contractile actin bundle running parallel to linear AJ in endothelial cells, but failed to precisely localize NMIIB (Efimova and Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Within 2 hr of releasing confinement, cells extended lamellipodia in random directions.
source: Within 2 hr, cells extended lamellipodia in random directions and approximately 50% of the pairs of cells contacted within 12 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from live imaging.

claim: Approximately 50% of the pairs of cells contacted within 12 hr after releasing confinement.
source: Within 2 hr, cells extended lamellipodia in random directions and approximately 50% of the pairs of cells contacted within 12 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from live imaging.

claim: The junction extended reaching a plateau at 40–45 µm length in around 3 hr.
source: The junction extended reaching a plateau at 40–45 µm length in around 3 hr (Figure 1c,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and 1e.

claim: GFP-E-cadherin accumulated at the edges of the junction.
source: As previously described (Yamada and Nelson, 2007), GFP-E-cadherin accumulated at the edges of the junction (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and citation to prior literature.

claim: In 98 +/- 2% of the cases, cell-cell contacts were stable and lasted above 3 hr and up to 22 hr.
source: Importantly, in 98 + /- 2% of the cases, cell-cell contacts were stable and lasted above 3 hr and up to 22 hr (Figure 1c,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and 1f.

claim: The centrosome relocalized towards the lamellipodia opposite to the cell-cell contact within one hour.
source: Analysis of the nucleus-centrosome axis relative to the junction axis showed a relocalization of the centrosome towards the lamellipodia opposite to the cell-cell contact within one hour (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d), as previously reported in different systems and cell types (Desai et al., 2009; Dupin et al., 2009; Burute et al., 2017; Rodríguez-Fraticelli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d and citations to prior literature.

claim: MDCK cells antipolarized in the doublet as if they were initiating a contact inhibition of locomotion.
source: However, although MDCK cells antipolarized in the doublet as if they were initiating a contact inhibition of locomotion, they remained attached to each other in contrast to more mesenchymal cells that proceed with cell separation following repolarization (Stramer and Mayor, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to prior literature.

claim: MDCK cells remained attached to each other in contrast to more mesenchymal cells that proceed with cell separation following repolarization.
source: However, although MDCK cells antipolarized in the doublet as if they were initiating a contact inhibition of locomotion, they remained attached to each other in contrast to more mesenchymal cells that proceed with cell separation following repolarization (Stramer and Mayor, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to prior literature.

claim: Y27-treated cells exhibited irregular junctions with small digitations and empty spaces.
source: Y27-treated cells exhibited irregular junctions with small digitations and empty spaces and did not elongate as much as control cells (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Y27-treated cells did not elongate junctions as much as control cells.
source: Y27-treated cells exhibited irregular junctions with small digitations and empty spaces and did not elongate as much as control cells (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Y27-treated cells were strongly affected in their capacity to maintain cell-cell contacts, half of the doublets separating before 3 hr.
source: They were strongly affected in their capacity to maintain cell-cell contacts, half of the doublets separating before 3 hr (Figure 1f,g and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f, 1g and Video 2.

claim: NMII activity is required for proper junction elongation and stabilization.
source: Similar results were observed after treating cells with the NMII ATPase activity inhibitor blebbistatin (data not shown) indicating that NMII activity is required for proper junction elongation and stabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with blebbistatin treatment.

claim: NMII was required for the centrosome repolarization.
source: Furthermore, NMII was required for the centrosome repolarization, as we could not observe any preferential orientation of the nucleus-centrosome axis in Y27-treated doublets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: NMIIA has been reported to be by large the major isoform of NMII expressed in MDCK cells.
source: NMIIA has been reported to be by large the major isoform of NMII expressed in MDCK cells (Ma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The three isoforms, NMIIA, NMIIB and NMIIC could be detected in MDCK cells by immunostaining.
source: However, immunostainings revealed that the three isoforms, NMIIA, NMIIB and NMIIC could be detected in MDCK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunostaining data.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIC fully co-localized to similar structures in MDCK cells.
source: NMIIA and NMIIC fully co-localized to similar structures, which was not the case for NMIIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIB did not fully co-localize with NMIIA and NMIIC in MDCK cells.
source: NMIIA and NMIIC fully co-localized to similar structures, which was not the case for NMIIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Stable transfection of specific ShRNA encoding plasmids led to an inhibition of NMIIA expression of around 60–70%.
source: Expression of each isoform was silenced in GFP-E-cadherin MDCK cells by stable transfection of specific ShRNA encoding plasmids, leading to an inhibition of expression of around 60–70% (Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Stable transfection of specific ShRNA encoding plasmids led to an inhibition of NMIIB expression of around 60–70%.
source: Expression of each isoform was silenced in GFP-E-cadherin MDCK cells by stable transfection of specific ShRNA encoding plasmids, leading to an inhibition of expression of around 60–70% (Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIB knock-down cells formed and extended intercellular junctions very similar to control cells.
source: The analysis of cell-cell contact formation in cell doublets by live-imaging (Video 3) revealed that NMIIB knock-down (NMIIB KD) cells formed and extended intercellular junctions very similar to control (Ctrl) cells (Figure 2c–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c–f and Video 3.

claim: Almost half of NMIIA knock-down cell doublets were unable to sustain contacts more than 3 hr.
source: In contrast, almost half of NMIIA knock-down (NMIIA KD) cell doublets were unable to sustain contacts more than 3 hr, and when they did so, these contacts remained shorter than for Ctrl or NMIIB KD cell doublets (Figure 2c–f), similar to what was observed in Y27-treated cell doublets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c–f.

claim: When NMIIA knock-down cell doublets sustained contacts, these contacts remained shorter than for Ctrl or NMIIB KD cell doublets.
source: In contrast, almost half of NMIIA knock-down (NMIIA KD) cell doublets were unable to sustain contacts more than 3 hr, and when they did so, these contacts remained shorter than for Ctrl or NMIIB KD cell doublets (Figure 2c–f), similar to what was observed in Y27-treated cell doublets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c–f.

claim: NMIIB KD doublets formed twisted junctions that were significantly less straight than Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells.
source: NMIIB KD doublets, despite their ability to maintain cell-cell contacts for longer times, formed twisted junctions that were significantly less straight than Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells and deviated significantly more from their initial orientation (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g,h.

claim: NMIIB KD doublets deviated significantly more from their initial orientation compared to Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells.
source: NMIIB KD doublets, despite their ability to maintain cell-cell contacts for longer times, formed twisted junctions that were significantly less straight than Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells and deviated significantly more from their initial orientation (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g,h.

claim: Defects in NMIIB KD cells were already observed at early stages of junction biogenesis and were associated to the formation of large extensions of junctional membrane.
source: These defects in NMIIB KD cells were already observed at early stages of junction biogenesis and were associated to the formation of large extensions of junctional membrane (Figure 2i, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Anti-NMIIA antibodies stained actin bundles that were parallel to the junction, setting at 1 to 2 μm from it, but did not stain the junctional area.
source: Immunostainings revealed a differential localization of the two isoforms relative to the junction. Anti-NMIIA antibodies stained actin bundles that were parallel to the junction, setting at 1 to 2 μm from it, but did not stain the junctional area.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data.

claim: NMIIA was found associated to actin cables parallel to the cortex of non-junctional membranes.
source: NMIIA was also found associated to actin cables parallel to the cortex of non-junctional membranes (Figure 3a,c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) in addition its association to the classical ventral stress fibres.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: NMIIB immunostaining was present on some perijunctional actin bundles.
source: NMIIB immunostaining was also present on some perijunctional actin bundles but, in contrast with NMIIA, was strongly associated with the junctional plasma membranes as well as with a cytoplasmic network (Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), that was identified as the vimentin intermediate filament network as reported by Menko and colleagues (Menko et al., 2014) in lens epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NMIIB was strongly associated with the junctional plasma membranes.
source: NMIIB immunostaining was also present on some perijunctional actin bundles but, in contrast with NMIIA, was strongly associated with the junctional plasma membranes as well as with a cytoplasmic network (Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), that was identified as the vimentin intermediate filament network as reported by Menko and colleagues (Menko et al., 2014) in lens epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NMIIB was associated with a cytoplasmic network identified as the vimentin intermediate filament network.
source: NMIIB immunostaining was also present on some perijunctional actin bundles but, in contrast with NMIIA, was strongly associated with the junctional plasma membranes as well as with a cytoplasmic network (Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), that was identified as the vimentin intermediate filament network as reported by Menko and colleagues (Menko et al., 2014) in lens epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b and citation to prior literature.

claim: The localization of each isoform was not affected by the silencing of the other isoform.
source: Importantly, the localization of each isoform was not affected by the silencing of the other isoform (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: NMIIA was associated to thick F-actin bundles running parallel to, and located a few microns away from the junctional membranes.
source: NMIIA was associated to thick F-actin bundles running parallel to, and located a few microns away from the junctional membranes (Figure 4a,c,d), as reported for NMIIA localization in linear junctions of endothelial cells (Hoelzle and Svitkina, 2012; Efimova and Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 4a,c,d and citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA did not colocalize with β−catenin-labeled cadherin-catenin complexes.
source: We confirmed at this resolution that NMIIA did not colocalize with β−catenin-labeled cadherin-catenin complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data.

claim: NMIIA appeared distributed on actomyosin bundles in sarcomere like structures.
source: Interestingly, NMIIA appeared distributed on actomyosin bundles in sarcomere like structures as described before in other cellular contexts (Choi et al., 2016; Ebrahim et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data and citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB junctional staining colocalizing with β−catenin was associated with a 200 nm to 1 µm thick fuzzy F-actin network.
source: NMIIB junctional staining colocalizing with β−catenin was associated with a 200 nm to 1 µm thick fuzzy F-actin network (Figure 4a–d), that also contained both Arp2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) and cortactin (Figure 5b–d), two known molecular markers of branched actin meshwork.
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 4a–d.

claim: The junctional F-actin network associated with NMIIB contained both Arp2/3 and cortactin.
source: NMIIB junctional staining colocalizing with β−catenin was associated with a 200 nm to 1 µm thick fuzzy F-actin network (Figure 4a–d), that also contained both Arp2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) and cortactin (Figure 5b–d), two known molecular markers of branched actin meshwork.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2e and Figure 5b–d.

claim: Arp2/3 and cortactin are known molecular markers of branched actin meshwork.
source: NMIIB junctional staining colocalizing with β−catenin was associated with a 200 nm to 1 µm thick fuzzy F-actin network (Figure 4a–d), that also contained both Arp2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) and cortactin (Figure 5b–d), two known molecular markers of branched actin meshwork.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Arp2/3 and cortactin.

claim: Short junctions that probably corresponded to nascent cell-cell contacts showed strong enrichment of NMIIB and the exclusion of NMIIA at the contact zone.
source: Looking at short junctions that probably corresponded to nascent cell-cell contacts, we could also observe the strong enrichment of NMIIB and the exclusion of NMIIA at the contact zone (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 4e,f.

claim: NMIIA KD cells exhibited shorter actin bundles running parallel to the junction.
source: NMIIA KD cells exhibited shorter actin bundles running parallel to the junction, while their juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork was comparable to the one of Ctrl cells, both in terms of morphology and cortactin staining (Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork of NMIIA KD cells was comparable to the one of Ctrl cells.
source: NMIIA KD cells exhibited shorter actin bundles running parallel to the junction, while their juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork was comparable to the one of Ctrl cells, both in terms of morphology and cortactin staining (Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIB KD cells presented a strongly enlarged area of junctional F-actin meshwork colocalizing with β−catenin.
source: In contrast, NMIIB KD cells presented a strongly enlarged area of junctional F-actin meshwork colocalizing with β−catenin that corresponded to overlapping membrane extensions stained with cortactin (Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 5a,e,f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIB KD cells retained some of the perijunctional actin bundles but had numerous oblique actin bundles directed toward the junction.
source: In addition, while they retained some of the perijunctional actin bundles, we could observe numerous oblique actin bundles directed toward the junction (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by SIM microscopy data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIA supports the organization of perijunctional actin bundles.
source: These results show that NMIIA supports the organization of perijunctional actin bundles while NMIIB contributes to restrain the extent of the juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork that couples perijunctional bundles to the plasma membrane, thus restraining lamellipodial activity at the junction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing shorter actin bundles in NMIIA KD cells.

claim: NMIIB contributes to restrain the extent of the juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork that couples perijunctional bundles to the plasma membrane.
source: These results show that NMIIA supports the organization of perijunctional actin bundles while NMIIB contributes to restrain the extent of the juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork that couples perijunctional bundles to the plasma membrane, thus restraining lamellipodial activity at the junction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing enlarged junctional F-actin meshwork in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIB restrains lamellipodial activity at the junction.
source: These results show that NMIIA supports the organization of perijunctional actin bundles while NMIIB contributes to restrain the extent of the juxtamembrane F-actin meshwork that couples perijunctional bundles to the plasma membrane, thus restraining lamellipodial activity at the junction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing large extensions of junctional membrane in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: An Arp2/3-nucleated actin network at the zonula adherens regulates junctional tension in epithelial monolayers.
source: An Arp2/3-nucleated actin network at the zonula adherens has been shown to regulate junctional tension in epithelial monolayers (Verma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Junctional tension has been shown to associate with the presence of α-catenin molecules under open conformations.
source: On the other hand, junctional tension has been shown to associate with the presence of α-catenin molecules under open conformations (Ishiyama et al., 2018; Yonemura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A direct link between α−catenin and NMIIB has been reported.
source: Moreover, a direct link between α−catenin and NMIIB has been reported (Vassilev et al., 2017), suggesting that NMIIB recruitment, α-catenin molecular unfolding and regulation of branched actin polymerization could be tightly linked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The ratio of α18 on total α−catenin junctional staining was decreased by four times in NMIIB KD cells compared to Ctrl cells.
source: Strikingly, the ratio of α18 on total α−catenin junctional staining was decreased by four times in NMIIB KD cells compared to Ctrl cells, while it was not affected in NMIIA KD cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining with α18 antibody.

claim: The ratio of α18 on total α−catenin junctional staining was not affected in NMIIA KD cells.
source: Strikingly, the ratio of α18 on total α−catenin junctional staining was decreased by four times in NMIIB KD cells compared to Ctrl cells, while it was not affected in NMIIA KD cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining with α18 antibody.

claim: Junctional α-catenin molecules were significantly turned to the closed conformational state in NMIIB KD cells.
source: This suggests that junctional α-catenin molecules were significantly turned to the closed conformational state in NMIIB KD cells (Figure 5g–i).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decreased α18/α-catenin ratio in NMIIB KD cells shown in Figure 5g–i.

claim: The total α-catenin junctional levels were significantly reduced in NMIIA KD cells.
source: In contrast, the total α-catenin junctional levels were significantly reduced in NMIIA KD cells, as shown by others (Shewan et al., 2005; Smutny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA KD cells spread 1.7 times more than Ctrl and NMIIB KD cells on fibronectin.
source: NMIIA KD cells spread 1.7 times more than Ctrl and NMIIB KD cells on fibronectin and their actin cytoskeleton was highly perturbed exhibiting a strong decrease in ventral stress fibres and cortical actin bundles together with an enlargement of their lamellipodia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton of NMIIA KD cells was highly perturbed exhibiting a strong decrease in ventral stress fibres and cortical actin bundles together with an enlargement of their lamellipodia.
source: NMIIA KD cells spread 1.7 times more than Ctrl and NMIIB KD cells on fibronectin and their actin cytoskeleton was highly perturbed exhibiting a strong decrease in ventral stress fibres and cortical actin bundles together with an enlargement of their lamellipodia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: NMIIA KD cells formed significantly less focal adhesions on fibronectin.
source: NMIIA KD cells also formed significantly less focal adhesions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,c.

claim: NMIIB KD cells showed no defect in actin organization, cell spreading or focal adhesion formation on fibronectin.
source: In contrast, NMIIB KD cells showed no defect in actin organization, cell spreading or focal adhesion formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: NMIIA KD cells exerted lower traction forces than Ctrl cells on fibronectin-coated 30 kPa PDMS gels.
source: NMIIA KD cells exerted lower traction forces than Ctrl cells as reported by others (Jorrisch et al., 2013; Shutova et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data and citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB KD cells did not show any defect in traction force generation on fibronectin-coated 30 kPa PDMS gels.
source: NMIIB KD cells, on the contrary, did not show any defect in traction force generation on this substratum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: NMIIA is the isoform regulating cell spreading, cell adhesion, traction force generation and organization of contractile actin structures on fibronectin.
source: These results, in agreement with previous studies (Jorrisch et al., 2013; Sandquist et al., 2006), show that NMIIA is the isoform regulating cell spreading, cell adhesion, traction force generation and organization of contractile actin structures on fibronectin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MNIIB is not contributing at all to the cell-matrix adhesion, focal adhesion formation, actomyosin reorganization and traction forces on fibronectin.
source: In contrary MNIIB is not contributing at all to the cell-matrix adhesion, focal adhesion formation, actomyosin reorganization and traction forces on fibronectin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no defects in NMIIB KD cells on fibronectin.

claim: Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells spread similarly on E-cadherin-coated substrates with mean areas of 1178 ± 40 µm² and 1031 ± 37 µm2 respectively.
source: After 6 hr, Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells had spread similarly with mean areas of 1178 ± 40 µm² and 1031 ± 37 µm2 respectively, while NMIIB KD cell spreading was significantly reduced (mean area = 515 ± 21 µm2) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: NMIIB KD cell spreading was significantly reduced on E-cadherin-coated substrates (mean area = 515 ± 21 µm2).
source: After 6 hr, Ctrl and NMIIA KD cells had spread similarly with mean areas of 1178 ± 40 µm² and 1031 ± 37 µm2 respectively, while NMIIB KD cell spreading was significantly reduced (mean area = 515 ± 21 µm2) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: Ctrl cells organized thick circumnuclear actin arcs, as well as radial actin fibres connected to peripheral β-catenin clusters on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: Ctrl cells organized thick circumnuclear actin arcs, as well as radial actin fibres connected to peripheral β-catenin clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a), as previously described (Gavard et al., 2004; Collins et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a and citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIA KD cells lacked the circumnuclear actin arcs and formed fewer large and small cadherin clusters on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: NMIIA KD cells, while spreading as Ctrl cells on E-cadherin lacked the circumnuclear actin arcs and formed fewer large and small cadherin clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,d.

claim: NMIIA KD cells could not organize large clusters aligned along actin cables on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: In particular they could not organize large clusters aligned along actin cables, as reported in MCF7 cells (Smutny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB KD cells kept the organization of circumnuclear actin arcs on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: NMIIB KD cells kept the organization of circumnuclear actin arcs, but were depleted of radial actin bundles, did not form significant β-catenin clusters and failed to spread on E-cadherin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d.

claim: NMIIB KD cells were depleted of radial actin bundles on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: NMIIB KD cells kept the organization of circumnuclear actin arcs, but were depleted of radial actin bundles, did not form significant β-catenin clusters and failed to spread on E-cadherin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d.

claim: NMIIB KD cells did not form significant β-catenin clusters on E-cadherin-coated substrates.
source: NMIIB KD cells kept the organization of circumnuclear actin arcs, but were depleted of radial actin bundles, did not form significant β-catenin clusters and failed to spread on E-cadherin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,c,d.

claim: NMIIB plays a major role in the clustering and stabilization of E-cadherin/catenin complexes that in turn promote cell spreading.
source: Contrasting with data obtained in MCF7 cells (Smutny et al., 2010), these data indicated that NMIIB plays a major role in the clustering and stabilization of E-cadherin/catenin complexes that in turn promote cell spreading.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced spreading and clustering in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIA is required for the formation of contractile actin fibres that apply traction forces on the cadherin adhesions.
source: Our findings also suggest that NMIIA is required for the formation of contractile actin fibres that apply traction forces on the cadherin adhesions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of circumnuclear actin arcs in NMIIA KD cells.

claim: NMIIA KD cells exhibited very low forces on E-cadherin substrate compared to Ctrl cells.
source: Compared to Ctrl cells, NMIIA KD cells exhibited very low forces on E-cadherin substrate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e,f), confirming that NMIIA generates the forces transmitted to E-cadherin adhesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2e,f.

claim: NMIIA generates the forces transmitted to E-cadherin adhesions.
source: Compared to Ctrl cells, NMIIA KD cells exhibited very low forces on E-cadherin substrate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e,f), confirming that NMIIA generates the forces transmitted to E-cadherin adhesions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM data showing very low forces in NMIIA KD cells on E-cadherin substrate.

claim: NMIIB KD cells generated lower traction forces than Ctrl cells on E-cadherin substrate, albeit to a lesser extent than NMIIA KD cells.
source: NMIIB KD cells, that failed to cluster cadherin/catenin complexes, also generated lower traction forces than Ctrl cells, albeit to a lesser extent than NMIIA KD cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2e,f.

claim: Both NMII isoforms contribute to cell-generated forces on E-cadherin substratum.
source: Even though both NMII isoforms contribute to cell-generated forces on E-cadherin substratum, they have complementary contributions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM data showing reduced forces in both NMIIA KD and NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIA is required for the formation of stress fibres.
source: NMIIA is required for the formation of stress fibres while NMIIB would rather regulate the transmission of force and the coupling of actin stress fibres to the cadherin-catenin complexes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of stress fibres in NMIIA KD cells.

claim: NMIIB regulates the transmission of force and the coupling of actin stress fibres to the cadherin-catenin complexes.
source: NMIIA is required for the formation of stress fibres while NMIIB would rather regulate the transmission of force and the coupling of actin stress fibres to the cadherin-catenin complexes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced clustering and force transmission in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: Hotspots of traction forces were generated at the periphery of the doublet where lamellipodia arise.
source: Hotspots of traction forces were generated at the periphery of the doublet where lamellipodia arise (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: NMIIA KD doublets exhibited lower traction forces both before and after cell-cell contact formation compared to Ctrl and NMIIB KD doublets.
source: As expected from the TFM data obtained with single cells seeded on fibronectin, NMIIA KD doublets, compared to Ctrl and NMIIB KD ones, exhibited lower traction forces both before and after cell-cell contact formation (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6a–c.

claim: NMIIB KD doublets developed traction forces similar in magnitude to those developed by Ctrl ones, with however different patterns.
source: NMIIB KD doublets developed traction forces similar in magnitude to those developed by Ctrl ones, with however different patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data.

claim: Hotspots of forces frequently appeared in the junctional area in NMIIB KD doublets that were generally absent in Ctrl and NMIIA doublets.
source: Hotspots of forces frequently appeared in the junctional area in NMIIB KD doublets that were generally absent in Ctrl and NMIIA doublets (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: NMIIB KD doublets generated higher F⊥ in the central part of the junction compared to Ctrl doublets.
source: NMIIB KD doublets generated higher F⊥ in the central part of the junction and lower values of F// with respect to Ctrl doublets in both the peripheral and the central part (albeit not significantly) of the junction (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: NMIIB KD doublets generated lower values of F// with respect to Ctrl doublets in both the peripheral and the central part of the junction.
source: NMIIB KD doublets generated higher F⊥ in the central part of the junction and lower values of F// with respect to Ctrl doublets in both the peripheral and the central part (albeit not significantly) of the junction (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: The ratios of parallel/perpendicular forces in the central and peripheral part of the junction were lower in NMIIB KD doublets compared to Ctrl doublets.
source: As a consequence, the ratios of parallel/perpendicular forces in the central and peripheral part of the junction were lower in NMIIB KD doublets compared to Ctrl doublets (Figure 6—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3c.

claim: NMIIB plays an important role in the repartition of traction forces in the junctional area at both cell-cell and cell-substrate interfaces.
source: The mechanical perturbation induced by knocking down NMIIB leads to a redistribution of transmitted forces in the junctional area at both cell-cell and cell-substrate interfaces. These results show that NMIIB plays an important role in the repartition of traction forces under the junction and that NMIIA is essential for the generation of traction forces in general.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM data showing altered force distribution in NMIIB KD doublets.

claim: NMIIA is essential for the generation of traction forces in general.
source: The mechanical perturbation induced by knocking down NMIIB leads to a redistribution of transmitted forces in the junctional area at both cell-cell and cell-substrate interfaces. These results show that NMIIB plays an important role in the repartition of traction forces under the junction and that NMIIA is essential for the generation of traction forces in general.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM data showing lower forces in NMIIA KD doublets.

claim: The net traction force exerted by an isolated doublet is zero, up to the measurement noise.
source: Following Newton's laws, the net traction force exerted by an isolated doublet is zero, up to the measurement noise.
evidence: This is based on Newton's laws of physics.

claim: The net traction forces exerted by each of the two cells in a doublet are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, compensating exactly.
source: Conversely, the net traction forces exerted by each of the two cells are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, compensating exactly (Liu et al., 2010; Maruthamuthu et al., 2011; Ng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on Newton's laws of physics and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The resultant force per cell before contact was within the level of noise as expected for isolated cells.
source: In all conditions, the resultant force per cell before contact was within the level of noise as expected for isolated cells and increased within 30 min after contact to reach a plateau, attesting the capacity of all three cell lines to transmit intercellular tugging forces across the junction (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: The resultant force per cell increased within 30 min after contact to reach a plateau in all three cell lines.
source: In all conditions, the resultant force per cell before contact was within the level of noise as expected for isolated cells and increased within 30 min after contact to reach a plateau, attesting the capacity of all three cell lines to transmit intercellular tugging forces across the junction (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: All three cell lines have the capacity to transmit intercellular tugging forces across the junction.
source: In all conditions, the resultant force per cell before contact was within the level of noise as expected for isolated cells and increased within 30 min after contact to reach a plateau, attesting the capacity of all three cell lines to transmit intercellular tugging forces across the junction (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM data showing increased resultant forces after contact in all cell lines.

claim: In NMIIA KD cells, the resultant forces per cell at the plateau was significantly lower than in Ctrl and NMIIB KD cell doublets.
source: However, in NMIIA KD cells, the resultant forces per cell at the plateau was significantly lower than in Ctrl and NMIIB KD cell doublets (Figure 6c), which is consistent with the inability of these cells to apply strong traction forces on fibronectin substratum.
evidence: This claim is supported by TFM data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Within 30 min after contact formation, the junction was submitted to a rise of σ⊥ in all three cell lines.
source: Within 30 min after contact formation, the junction was submitted to a rise of σ⊥ in all three cell lines, consistently with the emergence of a cell-cell tugging force (Figure 6—figure supplement 3d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3d,e.

claim: In Ctrl cells, the normal stress parallel to the junction σ//, remained higher than σ⊥.
source: However, in Ctrl cells, the normal stress parallel to the junction σ//, remained higher than σ⊥ (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: NMIIB KD and NMIIA KD cells exhibited equal amounts of normal stress parallel and perpendicular to the junction, denoting a more isotropic distribution of junctional tension.
source: Strikingly, this was not the case in NMIIB KD and NMIIA KD cells that exhibited equal amounts of normal stress parallel and perpendicular to the junction, denoting a more isotropic distribution of junctional tension (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB are both required for mechanical integrity of the junction.
source: Altogether, these results show that NMIIA and NMIIB are both required for mechanical integrity of the junction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM and stress tensor analysis data.

claim: NMIIA is necessary for generation of a high junctional inter-cellular stress through production of tugging forces compensated by traction applied at cell-matrix adhesions.
source: NMIIA is necessary for generation of a high junctional inter-cellular stress through production of tugging forces compensated by traction applied at cell-matrix adhesions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TFM and stress tensor analysis data showing lower forces and stress in NMIIA KD cells.

claim: NMIIB is necessary for the establishment of an anisotropic stress at the junction, sustaining high tension along the cell-cell interface.
source: NMIIB, on the other hand, is necessary for the establishment of an anisotropic stress at the junction, sustaining high tension along the cell-cell interface.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stress tensor analysis data showing isotropic stress in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB associate with distinct pools of actin during early steps of epithelial junction formation.
source: Here, we explore for the first time the involvement of NMII isoforms during early steps of epithelial junction formation. We show that NMIIA and NMIIB associate with distinct pools of actin and cooperate to initiate the formation of epithelial AJ before the acquisition of the apico-basal polarization (See Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: NMIIA and NMIIB cooperate to initiate the formation of epithelial AJ before the acquisition of the apico-basal polarization.
source: Here, we explore for the first time the involvement of NMII isoforms during early steps of epithelial junction formation. We show that NMIIA and NMIIB associate with distinct pools of actin and cooperate to initiate the formation of epithelial AJ before the acquisition of the apico-basal polarization (See Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: The existence of two distinct actin networks at adherens junctions had already been observed in early junctions between hepatocytes.
source: The existence of two distinct actin networks at adherens junctions had already been observed in early junctions between hepatocytes (Krendel and Bonder, 1999) and in endothelial cells where VE-cadherin was shown to colocalize with Arp2/3 complex-positive actin networks in-between distal actin-NMII bundles (Efimova and Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In endothelial cells, VE-cadherin was shown to colocalize with Arp2/3 complex-positive actin networks in-between distal actin-NMII bundles.
source: The existence of two distinct actin networks at adherens junctions had already been observed in early junctions between hepatocytes (Krendel and Bonder, 1999) and in endothelial cells where VE-cadherin was shown to colocalize with Arp2/3 complex-positive actin networks in-between distal actin-NMII bundles (Efimova and Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of α-catenin, the localization of NMIIB was not restricted any more to junctional membranes.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of α-catenin, the localization of NMIIB was not restricted any more to junctional membranes. Instead, NMIIB co-assembled with NMIIA on the same actin fibres, likely in heretotypic minifilaments, as observed in previous studies (Beach and Hammer, 2015; Shutova et al., 2017), indicating that α-catenin is responsible for the junctional recruitment of NMIIB, as reinforced by a recent publication reporting NMIIB and α-catenin interaction in glioblastoma cells (Vassilev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in α-catenin KD cells.

claim: In the absence of α-catenin, NMIIB co-assembled with NMIIA on the same actin fibres, likely in heretotypic minifilaments.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of α-catenin, the localization of NMIIB was not restricted any more to junctional membranes. Instead, NMIIB co-assembled with NMIIA on the same actin fibres, likely in heretotypic minifilaments, as observed in previous studies (Beach and Hammer, 2015; Shutova et al., 2017), indicating that α-catenin is responsible for the junctional recruitment of NMIIB, as reinforced by a recent publication reporting NMIIB and α-catenin interaction in glioblastoma cells (Vassilev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in α-catenin KD cells and citations to prior literature.

claim: α-catenin is responsible for the junctional recruitment of NMIIB.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of α-catenin, the localization of NMIIB was not restricted any more to junctional membranes. Instead, NMIIB co-assembled with NMIIA on the same actin fibres, likely in heretotypic minifilaments, as observed in previous studies (Beach and Hammer, 2015; Shutova et al., 2017), indicating that α-catenin is responsible for the junctional recruitment of NMIIB, as reinforced by a recent publication reporting NMIIB and α-catenin interaction in glioblastoma cells (Vassilev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data in α-catenin KD cells and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: E-cadherin complexes have been shown to biochemically interact with both Arp2/3 and NMIIB.
source: Given that E-cadherin complexes have been shown to biochemically interact with both Arp2/3 (Kovacs et al., 2002; Verma et al., 2012) and NMIIB (Vassilev et al., 2017), one hypothesis could be that NMIIB and Arp2/3 are both recruited to E-cadherin/catenin complexes upon cell-cell contact initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMIIB could serve as a cross-linker of the junctional actin network.
source: Given that E-cadherin complexes have been shown to biochemically interact with both Arp2/3 (Kovacs et al., 2002; Verma et al., 2012) and NMIIB (Vassilev et al., 2017), one hypothesis could be that NMIIB and Arp2/3 are both recruited to E-cadherin/catenin complexes upon cell-cell contact initiation. NMIIB could thus serve as a cross-linker of the junctional actin network.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: The absence of NMIIB may keep α-catenin in a closed conformation and induce a local softening of AJs which in turn leads to increased junctional lamellipodial extension.
source: Hence, the absence of NMIIB may keep α-catenin in a closed conformation and induce a local softening of AJs which in turn leads to increased junctional lamellipodial extension.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data showing decreased α18/α-catenin ratio and increased lamellipodial extensions in NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIB, by associating both with cadherin-catenin complexes and the branched actin, could somehow rigidify and regulate the thickness of the F-actin cushion sitting between the membrane and the contractile actin fibres associated to NMIIA.
source: NMIIB, by associating both with cadherin-catenin complexes and the branched actin, could somehow rigidify and regulate the thickness of this F-actin cushion sitting between the membrane and the contractile actin fibres associated to NMIIA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data showing NMIIB localization and the effects of NMIIB KD.

claim: NMIIB could rigidify the junctional actin network through the specific biochemical properties of NMIIB towards actin that provide it with the capacity to transmit tension within actin filaments at low energetic cost.
source: This could be achieved through the specific biochemical properties of NMIIB towards actin that provide it with the capacity to transmit tension within actin filaments at low energetic cost (Kovács et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and citations to prior literature about NMIIB biochemical properties.

claim: Within one hour of cell-cell contact, an anisotropic intercellular stress appeared at the junction, with a preferential orientation parallel to the junction, favoring the elongation and the stability of the nascent junction.
source: Within one hour of cell-cell contact, an anisotropic intercellular stress appeared at the junction, with a preferential orientation parallel to the junction, favoring the elongation and the stability of the nascent junction.
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis data.

claim: Both isoforms were required for proper establishment and orientation of intercellular stress.
source: Both isoforms were required for proper establishment and orientation of this intercellular stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stress tensor analysis data showing altered stress in both NMIIA KD and NMIIB KD cells.

claim: NMIIA silencing had a global impact on the amount of intercellular stress generated.
source: NMIIA silencing had a global impact on the amount of intercellular stress generated, which was not surprising given its role on traction force production both at cell-matrix and cell-cell adhesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by stress tensor analysis data showing reduced stress in NMIIA KD cells.

claim: NMIIB favored the production of a higher parallel intercellular stress, probably by driving the crosslinking and stiffening of the junctional actin network that couples the perijunctional contractile actin to the plasma membrane.
source: On the other hand, NMIIB favored the production of a higher parallel intercellular stress, probably by driving the crosslinking and stiffening of the junctional actin network that couples the perijunctional contractile actin to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stress tensor analysis data showing isotropic stress in NMIIB KD cells.
